enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B: PROGRAMMING (Population Growth Program)** *(30 marks)*

You are to write a program that determines how long it takes for a population to reach a particular size.

Suppose we have a population of *n* cows. Each year, *n/3* new cows are born, and *n/4* cows pass away. So, for example, if we have *n* = 1200 cows, then in the first year, 1200/3 = 400 new cows are born and 1200/4 = 300 cows pass away. Therefore, at the end of that year, we have 1200 + 400 - 300 = 1300 cows. Repeat the process with the new population size until the desired target population is reached.

Fractional cows in intermediate computations are discarded. So, for example, if there were 1001 cows initially, the number of new cows would be 1001/3 = 333.67 cows rounded down to 333 cows.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Task 4: Problem Understanding** *(6 marks)*

(i) Determine how long it will take for the population to grow from:

(a) 1200 to 1300 cows. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Apply the rule once: births = 1200/3 = 400, deaths = 1200/4 = 300, so the new size is 1200 + 400 - 300 = **1300**. The target is reached at the end of the first year.

| Year | Size at start (n) | n/3 (born, rounded down) | n/4 (die, rounded down) | Size at end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1200 | 400 | 300 | 1300 |

**Answer: 1 year.**

**Marking:** the correct answer with the births and deaths of the year shown (1).

questions.enonce_markdown: (i)(b) Determine how long it will take for the population to grow from 27 to at least 37 cows. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Repeat the yearly rule, **discarding fractions** at each step (27/3 = 9 exactly, but for example 33/4 = 8.25 gives 8 deaths), until the size is at least 37:

| Year | Size at start (n) | n/3 (born, rounded down) | n/4 (die, rounded down) | Size at end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 27 | 9 | 6 | 30 |
| 2 | 30 | 10 | 7 | 33 |
| 3 | 33 | 11 | 8 | 36 |
| 4 | 36 | 12 | 9 | 39 |

After 3 years the population is 36, which is still below 37; after the 4th year it is 39, which is at least 37. (Checked with a Python translation of the rule: the sizes are 27, 30, 33, 36, 39.)

**Answer: 4 years.**

**Marking:** the first two years correct (1); the sizes 36 and 39 reached (1); the conclusion of 4 years, noting that 36 does not reach 37 (1).

questions.enonce_markdown: (ii) How many years will it take for a population of 4 cows to become zero, if no new cows are born? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
With no births, the size at the end of a year is *n* - *n/4*, where *n/4* is rounded down.

| Year | Size at start (n) | n/4 (die, rounded down) | Size at end |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 1 | 3 |
| 2 | 3 | 0 | 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 0 | 3 |

From 4 cows the population falls to 3 in the first year. Then 3/4 = 0.75 cow, and fractional cows are discarded, so **no cow dies**: the size stays at 3 for ever (the sequence is 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, ... checked with a Python translation). In fact any population of 1, 2 or 3 cows is stable, because *n/4* rounds down to 0 for *n* < 4.

**Answer: it never becomes zero** (it stops decreasing at 3 cows after 1 year). Even if fractions were kept, 4 x (3/4)^t is positive for every *t*, so the population would still never be exactly zero.

**Marking:** the first year computed (3 cows) (1); the observation that 3 cows lose no cow, with the conclusion "never" (1).
